Question: Does a security guard have authority to give you a lifetime ban from a store? Or does the general store manager have to do it?
Answer: Anyone authorized by the store management can ban you from the store. If the store manager wants to give that power to his loss prevention/security people, their notice to you is completely enforceable.

Question: Why is the position of police chief a hired position and the position of sheriff is an elected one?
Answer: Most states (Connecticut and Alaska are exceptions) require each county or parish to have a sheriff. It’s in the state constitution, and sheriffs frequently describe themselves as “constitutional officers.” The sheriff is generally required to run a jail and provide security and process services to the courts. Law enforcement is a role they take on voluntarily. Some counties, particularly in the South, have county police departments separate from the sheriff’s department, leaving the sheriff with the jail and court duties only. Cities are not required to have police departments, and many don’t. The cities that don’t have their own police often contract with the local sheriff’s department to provide X deputies to patrol the town on a dedicated basis. The city can form a police department, of course. When they do, the chief of police generally reports to the mayor or city manager. One city I know of does elect their chief of police. Santa Clara, CA has done this for many years.

Question: Is it legal in Pa for law enforcement to limit the hours when a report can be filed? Our school district now has it's own internal police department. They are reportedly a legit dept. The issue is they are only open during school hours.
Answer: A school police department may not operate 24 hours per day, since the schools are usually daylight or daylight-evening operations. It is not reasonable for you to expect the school police to open after hours solely so you can make a report. Your report will be the same the following day, when the school police offices are open.

Question: When some US cops wrongfully arrest people over an argument over lack of probable cause, knowing that the person will be cleared, but not without paying bond or suffering days locked up in custody, isn't that precisely what the cop wants in revenge?
Answer: You seem to be describing what we used to call “contempt of cop.” Abuse the officer enough, and he will find some reason to arrest you. Making an arrest without probable cause is a career-ender. It opens the officer and his agency to civil lawsuits and federal civil rights claims, which will often result in the payment of six-figure damages. What separates contempt of cop from false arrest is discretion. Police officers have wide discretion in how to handle most situations in the field. Community policing training emphasizes that making an arrest is only one possible solution, and often is the least desirable option. There are many circumstances where an officer has more than enough probable cause for an arrest, but chooses some other path, to include warning the individual about their behavior and sending them on their way. Cops are human beings, and subject to the same emotional push buttons as everyone else. When the cop encounters someone who is being as obnoxious as possible toward the cop because they think they are immune from any enforcement action, it’s only natural for the cop to consider the option that will show Mr. Personality just how wrong he is about being immune. The cop might have to get creative, which means using the law in unconventional ways. There is nothing illegal about this, especially if Mr. P. has been warned about his behavior and the possible consequences. Example: we had both a state law and a city ordinance titled “Failure to obey a police officer.” Ominous as that might sound, it covered the behavior of people on the roadway. A police officer directing traffic can order motorists and pedestrians to move against posted directional signs of a one-way street, to stop where stopping is usually prohibited, and to do just about anything else to facilitate safety of traffic and people. If you’re a pedestrian on a public sidewalk, you have considerable freedom to walk, stop, or dance as you please, so long as you don’t impede others. Step onto the pavement, and the rules change. If the cop orders you to stop and get back on the sidewalk, that is an entirely lawful order. Refuse it, and you’re subject to citation or arrest. You can probably see where this is going. Say I’m on a traffic stop, and Mr. Personality happens by to engage in the exercise of his First Amendment rights. He shouts to everyone how I am a jackbooted thug (despite hearing that phrase so often, I never knew cops to wear jackboots, or run into many citizens who could describe them), how I am harassing an innocent civilian, and shouting unhelpful and mostly incorrect legal advice to my violator and the occupants of his car. I ask Mr. P. several times to tone it down, and he becomes more defiant. Eventually, he decides to move in a bit, and steps off the curb. I warn him to get back on the sidewalk. He comes back with some variation of “Whatcha gonna do about it, pig?” Bingo. Handcuffs time. Mr. P. gets to cool his heels in my prisoner cage while I finish the traffic stop. He may decide to resist arrest, which I and the other cops present will regard as quality entertainment and will result in additional charges. Then, he becomes a guest of the county detention facility, screaming all the way about his violated rights. He eventually gets to talk to a lawyer (despite their claims, these guys seldom have lawyers on retainer), who tells him he should have stayed on the sidewalk, and in the future, being less vocal during police operations would be advisable. There was lots of probable cause to arrest Mr. Personality. He created the situation himself.
